attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own post, giving his own estimate.

semantics.note: Faithful. It keeps the 'estimated' qualifier and the FY2025–FY2026 basis (32.3 + 74.4). He states a point estimate firmly, not as a probability, so it can be scored as an observation.

contract.note: Taking June 30, 2026 as the date and acquisition cost as the measure is an ordinary reading of his FY-based arithmetic. Treating the figure as approximate is fair to him. The packet cannot test the claim under any reasonable reading.

evidence.note: Microsoft's Q3 FY2026 remarks say about two-thirds of capex went to short-lived assets, mostly GPUs and CPUs. That covers one quarter's spending flow. It does not measure uninstalled GPU inventory or separate out CPUs.

reviews.rationale: The only item is a company statement on what one quarter's capex went to. The packet has no GPU-specific reconciliation of purchases against installations and no inventory value at June 30, 2026. The $106.7B estimate is neither confirmed nor shown to be badly off.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The revised proposition keeps 'it appears', 'quarter after quarter', the tens-of-billions scale and the 'only constrained' causal part. 'It appears' marks the claim as epistemically hedged, so it is not scored under policy.

contract.note: The contract itself says 'it appears' expresses uncertainty, yet it applies plain-reading support and contradiction tests. Policy limits plain-reading scoring to firm language, so the claim should be not_adjudicable rather than scored.

evidence.note: NVIDIA's Q2 FY2027 transcript gives $49B hyperscale revenue out of $96B total, about 51%. This backs only the over-50% component. It says nothing on hoarding or on what causes the supply constraint.
A secondary report that AWS took delivery of about $5B of racks in August ahead of available power. It covers one buyer, after the target quarter, and is not industry-wide or causal proof.

reviews.rationale: 'It appears' hedges the whole assertion, comparable to 'I suspect', so policy does not score it. For reference only, the evidence backs the over-50% revenue share and nothing more. It does not establish multi-quarter accumulation or that hyperscalers alone cause the constraint.

attribution.note: Zitron's own summary sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps 'for the most part', 'willingly or otherwise' and 'more effective'. The claim says coverage produces false beliefs, so causal is a fair kind. 'Everybody' is reasonably treated as emphasis.

contract.note: Reading 'laundering' as materially misleading presentation, without needing to prove intent, is ordinary. Requiring representative coverage and audience evidence is demanding but fits a 'for the most part' causal claim.

evidence.note: CNBC's body text says one Abilene building is operational. That matches Zitron's account that the disclosure sat below the headline. It does not show how representative the coverage is or how readers took it.
CNBC says seven buildings are online, with 30 planned. It shows partial completion was disclosed, which is consistent with his 'buried' framing, but it cannot show prevalence or effect on readers.

Amazon describes Rainier as a cluster spread across multiple data centers. An operating cluster and an unfinished campus can coexist. Whether that wording misleads is a matter of interpretation, not proof.

reviews.rationale: The packet covers only the two examples he named, and both articles disclose partial completion in their body text. There is no representative content analysis and no audience study. The evidence cannot settle how the press behaves for the most part or whether coverage causes outsiders to overestimate the buildout.

attribution.note: Zitron's own forecast in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Will, eventually' is an unhedged forecast with no deadline. The proposition keeps both the overcapacity clause and the too-late-to-notice clause.

contract.note: Reading the claim as a market-wide surplus relative to sustainable demand is the ordinary reading. The contract rightly says the open-ended forecast cannot be disproved by finite evidence, and its early-resolution rule is reasonable.

evidence.note: Cast AI found 5% average GPU utilization in non-optimized Kubernetes clusters, dated before the forecast. That reflects inefficiency in a selected sample, not a market-wide economic surplus.
Microsoft said in July 2026 that demand exceeds capacity. That is a company statement made before the forecast and cannot disprove eventual overcapacity.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was stated, and no dated, market-wide overcapacity episode with late recognition meets the early-resolution rule. The utilization data and Microsoft's demand statement are both context and do not settle the forecast.
